meta.title: Early warning signs of autistic meltdown — How to recognize them | Refugio Sensorial
meta.description: Learn to spot the bodily, cognitive, emotional, and behavioral signs before an autistic crisis. Act before you hit the limit.

articleTitulo: Early warning signs of autistic meltdown: how to recognize them
heading: Warning signs
sub: How to recognize a crisis is approaching before you hit the limit

corporales.tts: Your body starts warning you before you hit the limit. Pay attention to muscle tension in your shoulders, jaw, or hands. To pressure in your head. To your stomach churning or your heart racing. To increased sensitivity: when things you normally tolerate suddenly bother you a lot more. These are signs your nervous system is loading up, and the sooner you catch them, the easier it is to stop in time.
items: Muscle tension in shoulders, jaw, or hands
Headache or a feeling of pressure
Stomach discomfort or nausea
Increased sensitivity to light, sound, or touch
Sudden heat or cold with no clear cause
Racing heart or tight chest

cognitivas.tts: Your brain also sends warning signals before it gets overloaded. If you suddenly struggle to concentrate, process more slowly than usual, can't make simple decisions, or notice thoughts looping... that's not you failing. It's your cognitive system reaching its maximum capacity. Catching it and stopping early is much easier than recovering after a crisis.
items: Difficulty concentrating or following a train of thought
Slower processing than usual
Difficulty making small decisions
Thoughts that loop repeatedly
A feeling of mental fog
Difficulty speaking or expressing yourself fluently

emocionales.tts: When emotions start to dysregulate before a crisis, it usually shows up as irritability that doesn't quite make sense, floating anxiety, or a feeling that everything is too much. If things you can normally handle suddenly feel impossible, or you have quick emotional shifts you don't understand, your nervous system is probably already overloaded even if it doesn't look that way from the outside.
items: Disproportionate irritability over small things
Anxiety or restlessness with no clear cause
A feeling of overwhelm or that everything is too much
Quick emotional shifts that are hard to manage
A sense that everything takes more effort than usual
Difficulty regulating emotions with your usual strategies

conductuales.tts: Behavior also changes before a crisis. Maybe you're stimming more than usual because your body is trying to self-regulate. Or you feel you need to get away from people. Or talking becomes hard. Small changes might cost you more than usual, or a routine you normally follow without thinking now feels impossible. These are signs that your load is high and it's time to reduce it.
items: Increased stimming or an urgent need to move
Social withdrawal or a need to isolate
Reduced ability to speak or communicate
More rigidity or difficulty with changes
Difficulty following usual routines
Avoiding activities that are normally manageable

acciones.titulo: What to do when you notice them
acciones.subtitulo: Act before you hit the limit
acciones.tts: If you notice these signs, don't wait until you hit the limit. The time to act is now, while you still have resources to do it. Reduce stimuli, leave the environment if you can, use a regulation technique. If you're with someone you trust, tell them. Cancel or postpone what you can, without creating more stress. And above all: don't push yourself to keep functioning as if nothing's happening. Noticing the sign and stopping in time isn't giving up, it's taking care of yourself.
items: Leave the environment or reduce whatever stimuli you can
Use a regulation technique now, not once you hit the limit
Let someone you trust know if you're with company
Cancel or postpone what you can without creating more stress
Don't push yourself to keep functioning normally
Go to the Sensory Kit for quick regulation techniques
